imo-1960-01.title: Use the divisibility rule for 11
imo-1960-01.body:
Write $N=100a+10b+c$ with digits $a\ge1$, $b$, $c$. Divisibility by $11$ means $a-b+c\equiv 0\pmod{11}$, and since $-9\le a-b+c\le 18$, either $b=a+c$ or $b=a+c-11$.

**Case 1: $b=a+c$.** Then $N=110a+11c$, so $\frac N{11}=10a+c$ and the condition is
$$10a+c=a^2+(a+c)^2+c^2=2a^2+2ac+2c^2.$$
The right side is even, so $c$ is even. As a quadratic in $a$, $2a^2+(2c-10)a+(2c^2-c)=0$ needs a non-negative discriminant:
$$(2c-10)^2-8(2c^2-c)=-12c^2-32c+100\ge0\iff 3c^2+8c-25\le 0,$$
which forces $c\le 1$; with $c$ even, $c=0$. Then $2a^2-10a=0$, $a=5$, $b=5$: $N=550$. Check: $550/11=50=25+25+0$. ✓

**Case 2: $b=a+c-11$** (so $a+c\ge 11$). Then $N=110a+11c-110$, $\frac N{11}=10a+c-10$, and
$$10a+c-10=a^2+(a+c-11)^2+c^2.$$
Mod $2$ (using $k^2\equiv k$): the right side is $\equiv a+(a+c-11)+c\equiv 1$, the left side is $\equiv c$, so $c$ is odd. Expanding, $2a^2+(2c-32)a+(2c^2-23c+131)=0$, with discriminant
$$(2c-32)^2-8(2c^2-23c+131)=-12c^2+56c-24\ge 0\iff 3c^2-14c+6\le0,$$
which gives $0.48<c<4.2$, so $c\in\{1,3\}$.
- $c=1$: $a^2-15a+55=0$, discriminant $5$, no integer root.
- $c=3$: $a^2-13a+40=0$, $a\in\{5,8\}$; $a+c\ge11$ forces $a=8$, $b=0$: $N=803$. Check: $803/11=73=64+0+9$. ✓

**Answer: $550$ and $803$.**

imo-1960-01.title: Search over the quotient
imo-1960-01.body: Write $N=11k$ with $10\le k\le 90$, so $k$ is a sum of three squares of digits. A quick structured search: for $b=a+c$ we found $\frac N{11}=10a+c$, i.e. the quotient is "the number with digits $a,c$"; for $b=a+c-11$ the quotient is $10a+c-10$. Testing the few candidates allowed by the parity and size bounds above (or simply checking all $81$ multiples of $11$ between $110$ and $990$) gives exactly $550$ ($50=5^2+5^2+0^2$) and $803$ ($73=8^2+0^2+3^2$).

imo-1960-02.title: Substitute the square root
imo-1960-02.body:
The expression is defined when $1+2x\ge0$ and $\sqrt{1+2x}\ne1$, i.e. $x\ge-\frac12$ and $x\neq0$.

Let $t=\sqrt{1+2x}$, so $t\ge0$, $t\ne1$ and $2x=t^2-1$. Then
$$4x^2=(t^2-1)^2=(t-1)^2(t+1)^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{4x^2}{(1-t)^2}=(t+1)^2.$$
The inequality becomes
$$(t+1)^2<t^2-1+9\iff 2t+1<8\iff t<\frac72.$$
Thus $1+2x<\frac{49}{4}$, i.e. $x<\frac{45}{8}$.

**Answer:** $-\frac12\le x<\frac{45}{8}$ with $x\ne 0$.

imo-1960-02.title: Rationalise the denominator
imo-1960-02.body: For $x\ge-\frac12$, $x\ne0$: $\dfrac{2x}{1-\sqrt{1+2x}}=\dfrac{2x(1+\sqrt{1+2x})}{1-(1+2x)}=-(1+\sqrt{1+2x})$. Squaring, the left side equals $(1+\sqrt{1+2x})^2=2+2x+2\sqrt{1+2x}$. The inequality becomes $2+2\sqrt{1+2x}<9$, i.e. $\sqrt{1+2x}<\frac72$, i.e. $x<\frac{45}8$. Same answer.

imo-1960-03.title: Difference of angles from the altitude
imo-1960-03.body:
Let $O$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $H$ the foot of the altitude from $A$, so $AH=h$. Since $n$ is odd, the segment containing $O$ is the middle one, and it is centred at $O$: its endpoints $X,Y$ satisfy $OX=OY=\frac{a}{2n}$.

Use a coordinate $u$ along line $BC$ with origin $O$; then $X=-\frac a{2n}$, $Y=\frac a{2n}$, $H=d$ for some $d$. The angle that $AU$ (for $U$ on $BC$ at coordinate $u$) makes with $AH$ is $\theta(u)$ with $\tan\theta(u)=\frac{u-d}{h}$, $\theta\in(-90^\circ,90^\circ)$, and $\alpha=\theta(Y)-\theta(X)$. Hence
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{\frac{a/(2n)-d}{h}-\frac{-a/(2n)-d}{h}}{1+\frac{(a/(2n)-d)(-a/(2n)-d)}{h^2}}=\frac{\frac{a}{nh}}{1+\frac{d^2-a^2/(4n^2)}{h^2}}=\frac{ah/n}{h^2+d^2-\frac{a^2}{4n^2}}.$$
Now $h^2+d^2=AH^2+HO^2=AO^2$, and $AO=\frac a2$ because the midpoint of the hypotenuse is the circumcentre of the right triangle. Therefore
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{ah/n}{\frac{a^2}{4}-\frac{a^2}{4n^2}}=\frac{ah}{n}\cdot\frac{4n^2}{a^2(n^2-1)}=\frac{4nh}{(n^2-1)a}.$$
(The denominator is positive, confirming that $\alpha$ is acute.) ∎

imo-1960-03.title: Area and the law of cosines
imo-1960-03.body:
In triangle $AXY$ with $XY=\frac an$: twice its area is $XY\cdot h=AX\cdot AY\sin\alpha$, and by the law of cosines $AX^2+AY^2-XY^2=2AX\cdot AY\cos\alpha$. Dividing, $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{2\,XY\cdot h}{AX^2+AY^2-XY^2}$. By the median formula in triangle $AXY$ (with median $AO=\frac a2$), $AX^2+AY^2=2AO^2+\frac{XY^2}{2}=\frac{a^2}{2}+\frac{a^2}{2n^2}$. So
$$\tan\alpha=\frac{2ah/n}{\frac{a^2}{2}+\frac{a^2}{2n^2}-\frac{a^2}{n^2}}=\frac{2ah/n}{\frac{a^2(n^2-1)}{2n^2}}=\frac{4nh}{(n^2-1)a}.$$
∎

imo-1960-04.title: Two right triangles
imo-1960-04.body:
**Analysis.** Let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Triangle $AHM$ is right-angled at $H$ with $AH=h_a$ and hypotenuse $AM=m_a$, and its line $HM$ is the line $BC$. Moreover, since $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $B$ has distance $h_b$ from line $AC$, the point $M$ has distance $\frac{h_b}{2}$ from line $AC$. So line $AC$ is tangent to the circle with centre $M$ and radius $\frac{h_b}2$.

**Construction.**
1. Draw a line $\ell$, a point $H$ on it, the perpendicular at $H$, and $A$ on it with $AH=h_a$.
2. Draw the circle $(A,m_a)$; let $M$ be an intersection with $\ell$.
3. Draw the circle $\kappa$ with centre $M$ and radius $\frac{h_b}{2}$, and a tangent $t$ from $A$ to $\kappa$.
4. Let $C=t\cap\ell$ and let $B$ be the reflection of $C$ in $M$.

**Proof.** $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $AM=m_a$ is the median; $AH\perp BC$ with $AH=h_a$ is the altitude from $A$. The distance from $B$ to line $AC=t$ is twice the distance from $M$ to $t$ (as $C\in t$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $CB$), i.e. $2\cdot\frac{h_b}{2}=h_b$. ∎

**Discussion.** Step 2 needs $m_a\ge h_a$ (if $m_a=h_a$, then $M=H$ and the triangle is isosceles with $AB=AC$). Step 3 needs $A$ outside $\kappa$, i.e. $\frac{h_b}{2}<m_a$; then there are two tangents. Step 4 needs $t$ to meet $\ell$; a tangent is parallel to $\ell$ exactly when its distance from $M$, $\frac{h_b}{2}$, equals $h_a$, so for $h_b=2h_a$ only one tangent is usable. So, for $h_a<m_a$ and $h_b<2m_a$, $h_b\ne 2h_a$, there are two solutions (non-congruent in general); fewer in the boundary cases, and none if $m_a<h_a$ or $h_b\ge 2m_a$.

imo-1960-05.title: Coordinates
imo-1960-05.body:
Let the edge be $1$ and put
$$A=(0,0,1),\ B=(1,0,1),\ C=(1,1,1),\ D=(0,1,1),\quad A'=(0,0,0),\ B'=(1,0,0),\ C'=(1,1,0),\ D'=(0,1,0).$$
Then $X=(s,s,1)$ with $s\in[0,1]$ and $Y=(1-t,t,0)$ with $t\in[0,1]$, independently.

**(a)** The midpoint is
$$\Big(\frac{1+s-t}{2},\ \frac{s+t}{2},\ \frac12\Big).$$
It always lies in the plane $z=\frac12$. The map $(s,t)\mapsto\big(\frac{1+s-t}{2},\frac{s+t}{2}\big)$ is affine and injective, so it maps the unit square $[0,1]^2$ of parameters onto the parallelogram spanned by the images of its corners:
$$(0,0)\mapsto(\tfrac12,0),\ (1,0)\mapsto(1,\tfrac12),\ (1,1)\mapsto(\tfrac12,1),\ (0,1)\mapsto(0,\tfrac12).$$
These four points (at height $\frac12$) are the centres of the faces $ABB'A'$, $BCC'B'$, $CDD'C'$, $DAA'D'$. So the locus is the **square, including its interior,** with vertices at the centres of the four lateral faces (side $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$, sides parallel to $AC$ and $BD$).

**(b)** $ZY=2XZ$ means $Z=X+\frac13(Y-X)=\frac{2X+Y}{3}$:
$$Z=\Big(\frac{2s+1-t}{3},\ \frac{2s+t}{3},\ \frac23\Big).$$
Again an injective affine image of $[0,1]^2$, a parallelogram in the plane $z=\frac23$ (one third of the edge below the face $ABCD$) with vertices
$$(0,0)\mapsto(\tfrac13,0),\ (1,0)\mapsto(1,\tfrac23),\ (1,1)\mapsto(\tfrac23,1),\ (0,1)\mapsto(0,\tfrac13).$$
Its sides are $(\frac23,\frac23)$ (i.e. $\frac23\overrightarrow{AC}$) and $(-\frac13,\frac13)$ (i.e. $\frac13\overrightarrow{BD}$), which are perpendicular. So the locus is the **filled rectangle** in the plane $z=\frac23$, centred at $(\frac12,\frac12,\frac23)$ on the vertical axis of the cube, with sides of length $\frac23AC=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$ parallel to $AC$ and $\frac13BD=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$ parallel to $BD$. ∎

imo-1960-06.title: Express both volumes through the base angle
imo-1960-06.body:
Take the axial cross-section: an isosceles triangle with base $2R$ (the base diameter), height $H$, base angles $\beta$ ($0<\beta<90^\circ$), and its incircle of radius $r$ (the section of the sphere). The cylinder has radius $r$ and height $2r$, so $V_2=2\pi r^3$, while $V_1=\frac13\pi R^2H$.

The incentre lies on the bisector of the base angle, so $r=R\tan\frac\beta2$; also $H=R\tan\beta$. With $t=\tan\frac\beta2\in(0,1)$ we have $\tan\beta=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}$, hence
$$V_1=\frac{\pi R^3}{3}\cdot\frac{2t}{1-t^2},\qquad V_2=2\pi R^3t^3,\qquad \frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{1}{3t^2(1-t^2)}.$$
Let $w=t^2\in(0,1)$. By AM–GM, $w(1-w)\le\frac14$, with equality iff $w=\frac12$. Therefore
$$\frac{V_1}{V_2}=\frac{1}{3w(1-w)}\ge\frac43.$$

**(a)** $V_1=V_2$ would need $w(1-w)=\frac13>\frac14$, impossible. So $V_1\ne V_2$.

**(b)** The ratio $k=V_1/V_2$ takes every value $\ge\frac43$ and the smallest is $k=\frac43$, attained for $\tan^2\frac\beta2=\frac12$. Then $\tan\beta=\frac{2/\sqrt2}{1/2}=2\sqrt2$, so $\cos\beta=\frac13$. The angle $\gamma$ at the vertex (subtended by a base diameter) is $180^\circ-2\beta$, so
$$\sin\frac\gamma2=\cos\beta=\frac13,\qquad \cos\gamma=1-2\sin^2\frac\gamma2=\frac79.$$
**Construction:** draw a right triangle with hypotenuse $3$ and one leg $1$; the angle opposite the leg $1$ is $\frac\gamma2$; doubling it (reflect the triangle in its longer leg) gives $\gamma$.

**Answer:** $k=\frac43$; the vertex angle $\gamma$ satisfies $\sin\frac\gamma2=\frac13$. ∎

imo-1960-07.title: Coordinates and a dot product
imo-1960-07.body:
Place the trapezoid with base $a$ on the $x$-axis and the axis of symmetry as the $y$-axis:
$$A=\big(-\tfrac a2,0\big),\ B=\big(\tfrac a2,0\big),\ C=\big(\tfrac c2,h\big),\ D=\big(-\tfrac c2,h\big),$$
with legs $BC$ and $DA$. Let $P=(0,y)$.

**(a)** The leg $BC$ subtends a right angle at $P$ iff $\overrightarrow{PB}\cdot\overrightarrow{PC}=0$:
$$\frac a2\cdot\frac c2+(-y)(h-y)=0\iff y^2-hy+\frac{ac}{4}=0.$$
By the symmetry in the axis, the leg $DA$ then also subtends a right angle at $P$. So the points are $P=(0,y)$ with
$$y=\frac{h\pm\sqrt{h^2-ac}}{2}.$$
Geometrically: $P$ is an intersection of the axis with the circle having diameter $BC$.

**(b)** The distance from $P$ to the base $a$ is $y=\frac{h\pm\sqrt{h^2-ac}}{2}$, and to the base $c$ it is $h-y=\frac{h\mp\sqrt{h^2-ac}}{2}$. (Both roots have sum $h$ and positive product $\frac{ac}4$, so both lie strictly between the bases.)

**(c)**
- $h^2>ac$: two points $P$, symmetric with respect to the midline of the trapezoid.
- $h^2=ac$: exactly one point, at height $\frac h2$ (the circle on $BC$ is tangent to the axis). This is exactly the case in which the trapezoid has an inscribed circle: the leg is $\sqrt{h^2+\frac{(a-c)^2}{4}}$, and the Pitot condition $2\cdot\text{leg}=a+c$ is equivalent to $h^2=ac$; then $P$ is the incentre.
- $h^2<ac$: no such point. ∎
